paper_metadata.title: Space and Time Cost of Continuous Rotations in Surface Codes

summary: This paper is a surface-code resource study of continuous-rotation implementations, comparing conventional Clifford+T synthesis with catalyst towers for two use cases: a phase oracle with S=36 and n=15, and repeated Gaussian-state preparation using 60 copies of a 5-qubit, 7-layer Ry-CNOT circuit. The reported metrics are resource counts and depths only: measurement depths of 32, 62, and 17 for gate synthesis, in-circuit towers, and independent towers in the oracle case, and an expected depth of 39 with T-counts of 28,709 or 45,750 per repetition for the Gaussian-state case.

experiments.description: Surface-code resource analysis of in-circuit catalyst towers versus conventional Clifford+T synthesis for a parallel piecewise phase oracle used in an option-pricing subroutine.

algorithm.variant: in-circuit catalyst towers for continuous rotations in a phase oracle

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Option-pricing phase oracle on n=15 input qubits with piecewise linear function split into S=36 pieces; fan-out via GHZ states to parallelize oracle evaluation.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Implement |x⟩ → exp(i f(x)) |x⟩ for a piecewise linear payoff/oracle function f(x) in an option-pricing algorithm.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Parallel fan-out/fan-in, logical-AND gates, AutoCCZ-based Toffoli construction, lattice-surgery routing; no penalty formulation.

problem_instance.description: Derivative-pricing / option-pricing subroutine using a low-depth phase oracle.

dataset_specification.description: Parameters taken from the option-pricing setting of ref. [5]; S=36, n=15, l=6.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Analytical resource estimation and comparison across code distances; no empirical sampling runs reported for this experiment.

transpilation_settings.routing_method: lattice surgery / long-range CNOT via ref. [24]

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Piecewise oracle decomposition; GHZ-state fan-out prepared before runtime; parameter choices fixed from ref. [5].

speedup_claims.factor: lower spacetime volume up to code distance ~13; about 2x faster beyond threshold
speedup_claims.conditions: for the option-pricing phase oracle in a surface-code architecture; low-to-intermediate code distances, with crossover around d≈13 and direct gate synthesis outperforming above d≈16
speedup_claims.caveats: Benefits are specific to the chosen option-pricing parameters and routing assumptions; at large code distances conventional synthesis becomes more efficient.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Resource scaling analyzed in terms of physical qubits and spacetime volume; independent towers have depth scaling logarithmically in S and n.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Analytical resource estimates for logical qubits, physical qubits, and spacetime volume; no runtime benchmark against a classical solver.
limiting_factors: No classical runtime baseline for the oracle implementation
Comparison is only among gate-synthesis and catalyst-tower layouts
Advantage is framed as reduced spacetime volume, not end-to-end quantum advantage

notes: No specific QPU or simulator is named; this is a resource-estimation study on surface-code architecture, so hardware.type is not specified.
The paper reports logical-qubit formulas and code-distance-dependent physical-qubit counts rather than a single fixed qubit number, so num_qubits is inferred as not fixed/reported.
The paper reports measurement depths (32, 62, 17) and spacetime-volume comparisons, but not a single circuit depth for the full experiment.
No asymptotic quantum speedup over classical algorithms is characterized; the paper only compares resource costs across implementations.
The paper reports only resource comparisons for surface-code implementations of a phase oracle.
It does not demonstrate a practical quantum advantage over classical methods.

experiments.description: Surface-code resource analysis of independent catalyst towers versus conventional Clifford+T synthesis for repeated Gaussian-state preparation via a variational Ry-CNOT circuit used in the option-pricing workflow.

algorithm.variant: variational Ry-CNOT state-preparation circuit with independent catalyst towers and RUS teleportation
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Classically trained Ry-CNOT ansatz from ref. [31].

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Continuous rotations implemented as Ry(θ)=S H Rz(θ) H S†; 60 independent 5-qubit circuit copies prepared in parallel.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Prepare quantum states whose amplitudes follow a normal distribution for use in derivative-pricing amplitude-estimation workflows.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: RUS teleportation of rotation resource states; control and excess tower schemes to match geometric distribution of required resource states.

problem_instance.description: Gaussian state preparation for 60 copies of a 5-qubit variational circuit in a derivative-pricing algorithm.

dataset_specification.description: 60 copies of a 5-qubit, 7-layer Ry-CNOT circuit; amplitudes follow a standard normal distribution.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Classical training of the variational circuit to approximate a normal distribution; then repeated coherent copies are used in the pricing workflow.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Analytical resource estimation; expected depth estimated numerically with 10,000 samples for the RUS completion-time distribution.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical training of the variational ansatz; produce-and-store strategy for resource states; control and excess tower constructions for RUS matching.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Expected depth estimated by numerical simulation over 10,000 samples; resource counts compared across gate synthesis and tower schemes.

speedup_claims.conditions: for code distances below 10 in Gaussian state preparation with independent catalyst towers
speedup_claims.caveats: The excess scheme uses fewer physical qubits while being faster; advantages depend on code distance and the produce-and-store strategy.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Resource scaling analyzed via T-count, T-depth, and physical-qubit count; independent towers reduce depth and can reduce spacetime volume at low code distances.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Analytical estimates of T-count, expected measurement depth, and physical-qubit count for repeated Gaussian-state preparation; no end-to-end classical-vs-quantum benchmark.
limiting_factors: The paper compares gate synthesis vs catalyst towers only
Reported gains are resource-efficiency gains, not demonstrated application-level advantage

notes: This is a surface-code resource-estimation study, not an execution on a named QPU or simulator.
The paper reports 5 qubits per circuit copy and 60 copies, but not a single fixed total qubit count because the physical/logical footprint depends on code distance and tower layout.
The paper explicitly reports 7 layers and 35 parametrized Ry rotations per copy; the 10,000-sample numerical simulation is for expected depth estimation, not quantum shots on hardware.
No asymptotic speedup over classical algorithms is claimed; only resource-efficiency comparisons are made.
The paper reports analytical resource estimates for repeated rotations in a variational circuit.
It does not demonstrate practical quantum advantage over classical methods.
